extracted.intended_audience: broadband policy stakeholders (industry groups, local governments, regulators, policy watchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on policy proposals and stakeholder positions about whether the FCC should preempt state and local permitting rules by imposing a 60‑day 'shot clock' (and related conditions such as bulk permitting prohibitions) for wireline infrastructure rights-of-way and permit approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60-day shot clock for state and local permitting agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute a 60-day shot clock for state and local permitting agencies to respond to standard permit and rights-of-way requests, after which the applications would be deemed granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requested by eight trade groups (USTelecom, NCTA, CTIA, INCOMPAS, et al.) as a mechanism to speed approvals; similar language appears in a House Commerce Committee bill introduced by Rep. Buddy Carter. The proposal applies to 'standard permit and rights-of-way requests' and contemplates automatic approval if no response within 60 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deem applications granted after shot clock expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: If the permitting agency does not respond within the 60-day period, the application would be treated as granted (i.e., deemed approved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'deemed granted' enforcement mechanism is central to industry filings arguing for timeliness; it is presented as a remedy for alleged 'unnecessarily long wait times' and delays in network deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit restrictions on bulk permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit local restrictions on bulk permitting (allowing firms to obtain multiple permits/batch authorizations) as part of conditions accompanying preemption or shot-clock rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry groups explicitly asked the FCC to bar restrictions on bulk permitting and to 'impose other conditions' to facilitate large-scale deployments; the request frames bulk-permitting bans as an unnecessary barrier to rapid buildout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption where local regulations effectively prohibit broadband deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use authority under the Communications Act to overrule state and local regulations that 'effectively prohibit broadband deployment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FCC's statutory preemption power is invoked by industry as justification for federal intervention; the FCC voted to open an inquiry into state and local wireline permitting rules that it 'could preempt' under the Act. Whether a rule 'effectively prohibits' deployment is thus a legal threshold for preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether procedural requirements are overburdensome or unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate local/state permitting procedures for being 'overburdensome and unnecessary' — e.g., fragmented policymaking, excessive procedural requirements, long wait times, and excessive fees that hinder infrastructure deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry filings frame decades of fragmented policymaking and excessive fees/wait times as evidence that federal action is needed; this criterion focuses on procedural burden as a justification for preemption or shot-clock rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect public safety and rights-of-way asset management through permit reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments assert permit reviews are necessary to ensure public safety and to responsibly manage public assets in the rights-of-way; these reviews should not be unduly curtailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local government associations (U.S. Conference of Mayors, National League of Cities, National Association of Counties, NATOA) argue that permit reviews are reasonable, often conducted with limited staffing, and are necessary to prevent harms (citing a report of >12,000 gas line strikes from 2021–2023). They object to measures that would 'strip local governments of their ability to responsibly manage public assets in the rights-of-way.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on FCC legal authority to preempt reasonable local permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Preemption should be constrained by the FCC's legal authority; the FCC may lack authority to preempt reasonable local permitting processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local stakeholders contend the FCC does not have legal authority to preempt local permitting where reviews are reasonable and necessary. This is presented as a separate legal standard from the 'effective prohibition' test: even if deployment concerns exist, preemption must fit within statutory limits and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State broadband price regulation not preemptable if not a meaningful barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws regulating broadband rates (e.g., New York's Affordable Broadband Act mandating $15/$20 pricing for low-income households) are not preemptable under the Communications Act if they are not a meaningful barrier to network deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACA Connects and NCTA asked the FCC to preempt such state laws; the New York State PSC defended its law, arguing it 'wasn’t a meaningful barrier to broadband network deployment' and therefore cannot be preempted. The article notes the law contains exemptions for ISPs with under 20,000 subscribers and that industry legal challenges failed up to the Supreme Court declining review.
